newsitem.title: USA: Clinton, Gore promote Internet on radio.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Gore promote Internet on radio.

text.p: President Bill Clinton and Vice President Al Gore went to the radio airwaves Saturday on behalf of increasing access to cyberspace in American schools.

Appearing jointly in the president's weekly radio address, they announced the number of schools connected to the Internet has nearly doubled in the last two years to 65 percent but said the job is far from over.
"It's not enough to connect every school," Clinton said. "We must connect every classroom and every library as well."
He said the number of actual classrooms rigged up for Internet access has quadrupled since 1994 but that, according to a new Education Department report, "the vast majority still do not have access."

Gore said the Education Department would award Technology Literacy Challenge Grants totalling $14.3 million to Illinois, Mississippi and New Mexico to equip classrooms with computers, link schools to the Internet and train teachers.

The grants are the first under a programme that will spend $200 million this year. Clinton's proposed $51 billion education budget for the fiscal year starting next Oct. 1 would provide $500 million for computers, teacher training and educational software, most of it in grants.
"Altogether, this is an unprecedented effort to connect the children of this century to the technology of the next," Gore said.

In the Republican radio address, Sen. Don Nickles, R-Okla., said Republicans agree on the need to improve education for children and get crime and drugs out of schools, "but we do question the wisdom of just adding more federal programmes."
An advance text of Nickles' address attacked specifically "the new Internet programme he and Vice President Gore announced this morning," but on delivery he deleted the phrase.
A Nickles spokesman, Brook Simmons, said Nickles took out the phrase because he wanted to speak about federal education programmes in general.
During last year's presidential campaign, Republican nominee Bob Dole found it hard to attack many Clinton high-tech proposals that are popular with the public.

Clinton has made connecting schools to the Internet a major part of what he called in his State of the Union speech Tuesday night a "national crusade" to improve America's public education system going into the 21st century.
He and Gore last March staged "NetDay96" in California to promote the effort to connected 4,000 schools in that state to the Internet.
This year, Clinton said in his radio remarks, on April 19 NetDays will be held in all 50 states with the goal of "connecting tens of thousands of schools, classrooms and libraries to the Internet."

Since many schools find it prohibitively expensive to sign up with on-line companies, Clinton urged the Federal Communications Commission act quickly to develop a plan under the year-old Telecommunications Act to give schools and libraries Internet access at a dramatically discounted rate.
He called on the telecommunications industry to support the effort.
